name: Isaiah
sourceNote: Written freshly, thought for thought, from the oldest Hebrew, Greek, and Aramaic witnesses (the Masoretic Text with the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, and the Samaritan Pentateuch). © 2026 Jose Santiago. All rights reserved.

verses.text: Isaiah{a} son of Amoz saw a vision about Judah and Jerusalem. It came during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah over Judah.

Sky, hear this! Earth, lean in close!
Yahweh has something to say:
“Sons and daughters were fed and raised in my home.
Now they have fought against their own father.

An ox recognizes the one who owns it.
A donkey finds the feeding box of its master.
But Israel{b} does not recognize me.
My own people do not understand.”

Shame on this sinful nation,
weighed down by its wrongs,
a brood of troublemakers,
sons who destroy.
They left Yahweh behind.
They sneered at the Holy One of Israel
and walked off in the other direction.

Where else will I strike you?
You keep on turning against me.
Every part of your head aches,
and every beat of your heart is faint.

You have no healthy spot at all,
not from your toes up to your scalp.
It is all bruises, gashes, and raw wounds,
not wiped clean, not wrapped,
not eased with oil.

Your land lies in ruins.
Fire has destroyed your cities.
Strangers eat the crops of your fields
while you stand and watch.
The land is as bare as a place that foreigners have wrecked.

The city of Zion{c} is left standing alone,
like a shed in a vineyard,
like a hut in a field of cucumbers,
like a town surrounded by enemies.

Yahweh of Armies{d} left a few of us alive.
If he had not,
we would have ended up like Sodom,
and we would be just like Gomorrah.{e}

Listen to what Yahweh says,
you chiefs who rule like Sodom.
Hear our God’s instruction,{f}
you crowd who act like Gomorrah.

“What good are your many offerings to me?” Yahweh asks.
“I have had enough of rams burned whole
and of the fat from fattened calves.
Blood from bulls, lambs, and goats does not please me.

Who told you to come and tramp through my courtyards
every time you appear before me?

Stop bringing worthless gifts.
Your incense disgusts me.
I cannot stand your New Moon feasts, your Sabbaths,
or your meetings,
because you mix them with wickedness.

Your feasts at the new moon and your appointed holidays
are things my whole being despises.
They have turned into a load on my back.
I am worn out from holding it up.

You spread out your hands toward heaven,
but I will cover my eyes.
You may offer prayer after prayer,
yet I will not hear one,
for blood drips from your hands.{g}

Scrub yourselves until you are clean.
Remove your wicked actions from in front of me.
Quit doing evil.

Learn to do good.
Look for what is fair.
Help those who are being crushed.{h}
Stand up for children who have no father.
Speak for the widow in her fight.”

“Come now, let us talk this over,” says Yahweh.
“Your sins are as red as dark red cloth,
but they can become as white as snow.
They are as bright as crimson dye,
but they can become like clean wool.{i}

Say yes and listen,
and you will feast on the land’s finest food.

Say no and fight me,
and swords will feast on you.”
Yahweh’s own mouth has spoken.

Look at the loyal city!
She has become like a woman who sells herself.
She used to be full of justice,
and fairness made its home in her.
Now killers live there.

Your silver has turned into waste metal.
Your wine has been watered down.

Your leaders are rebels who go around with thieves.
Each one loves gifts
and runs after payments.
They do not stand up for children who have no father.
The widow’s case never even reaches them.

So the Lord, Yahweh of Armies,
the Strong One of Israel,{j} says:
“I will get relief from my opponents
and settle accounts with my foes.

I will give you judges again, as you had at the start,
and advisers as you had long ago.
After that you will be called the City of Justice,
the Loyal City.”

Zion will be bought back by fairness.
Those in her who turn back will be saved by doing right.{l}

Rebels and sinners will all be shattered together,
and anyone who abandons Yahweh will be finished.

The sacred oaks you cherished will bring you shame,
and the gardens you picked will make you blush.{m}

You will be like an oak whose leaves dry up,
like a garden without any water.

The mighty one will become tinder,
and what he made will become the spark.
Both will go up in flames at once,
and nobody will be there to put it out.{n}

notes.text: “Isaiah” in Hebrew means “Yahweh saves.” Amoz means “strong.” He is not the same as the prophet Amos. These kings ruled from about 790 to 686 BC.
Israel means “he struggles with God” or “God fights.” Here it means the whole people.
Zion is the hill in Jerusalem where the Temple stood. Its meaning is uncertain. “City of Zion” is a poetic way to speak of the people of Jerusalem.
Hebrew YHWH Tseva’ot, often translated “the LORD of hosts.” It means Yahweh is the commander of all armies, both on earth and in heaven.
Sodom and Gomorrah were the cities that God destroyed in Genesis 19. Their names’ meanings are uncertain.
Hebrew torah, which can mean “teaching” or “law.” Here it is the message of the prophet.
The Great Isaiah Scroll (one of the Dead Sea Scrolls) adds “and your fingers are full of guilt,” as in 59:3.
Or “correct those who are cruel.” The Septuagint says “rescue the one who is wronged.” The Hebrew word is unclear.
The Hebrew can also be read as a question: “Though your sins are red, can they become white as snow?”
The first title is Hebrew ha’adon, “the master” or “the Lord.” “Strong One of Israel” is Hebrew ‘avir Yisra’el. Compare “Strong One of Jacob” in Genesis 49:24.
Or “wash away your waste with lye.” The base metals mixed into silver, such as tin or lead, were removed when it was refined.
Or “those in her who repent.”
The oaks and gardens were places where people worshiped false gods and asked for good harvests.
Or “the strong man.” With different vowels some read “your strength” and “your work.” The Great Isaiah Scroll reads it that way.

subheads.21: The City That Lost Its Way

verses.text: This is the message that Isaiah son of Amoz received about Judah and Jerusalem.

In the last days
the mountain that holds Yahweh’s house
will stand taller than every other mountain.
It will rise above all the hills,
and people from every nation will stream toward it.{a}

Many peoples will set out, saying,
“Come, let us go up Yahweh’s mountain,
to the house of Jacob’s God.{b}
He will show us his ways,
and we will walk the paths he marks out.”
Zion will send out his teaching,
and Jerusalem will send out Yahweh’s word.{c}

He will settle quarrels between nations
and decide cases for many peoples.
They will pound their swords into plow blades
and turn their spears into tools for trimming vines.
Nations will stop attacking each other,
and no one will train for war anymore.

People of Jacob, come!
Let us walk in the light of Yahweh.

Their land is full of silver and gold,
and their treasure never runs out.
Their land is full of horses,
and their chariots cannot be counted.

Go into the rocks.
Hide in the dirt
from the terror of Yahweh
and the shining glory of his greatness.{h}

Proud eyes will be lowered.
Arrogant people will be brought down.
On that day only Yahweh will be lifted high.

Yahweh of Armies has a day planned
against everything proud and high,
against everything that lifts itself up,
and it will be brought low.

It is against all the cedars of Lebanon, tall and lofty,
and against all the oak trees of Bashan.{i}

It is against all the high mountains
and all the raised-up hills.

It is against every tall tower
and every strong wall.

It is against all the ships of Tarshish{j}
and every beautiful boat.

Human pride will be bent down,
and arrogant people will be brought low.
On that day only Yahweh will be lifted high.
The idols will disappear completely.

People will slip into rock caves
and burrow into pits in the dust,
running from the terror of Yahweh
and his majestic glory
on the day he gets up and makes the earth tremble.

When that day comes, everyone will fling away
the silver and gold statues
they had crafted for worship.
They will leave them for moles and bats.{k}

They will squeeze into cracks in the rocks
and holes in the cliffs,
running from the terror of Yahweh
and his majestic glory,
on the day he gets up and makes the earth tremble.

notes.text: Verses 2-4 are almost the same as Micah 4:1-3.
Jacob means “he grabs the heel” or “he cheats.” Here it means the people who came from him.
Or “instruction” (Hebrew torah).
The Philistines lived on the southern coast of Canaan.
Hebrew “they clap hands with the children of foreigners.” It means making agreements. The first line may also be “full of fortune-tellers from the east.” Some words may have dropped out.
Hebrew ‘elilim, a scornful word for idols. It sounds like ‘elohim (“God”) and means “nothings.”
Or “and you cannot lift them up.” The Great Isaiah Scroll leaves out the last line of verse 9 and all of verse 10. The Septuagint has both.
Compare Revelation 6:15-16.
Lebanon means “white,” a snowy mountain range north of Israel. Bashan was the green highland east of the Sea of Galilee.
Tarshish was a far-off port in the west, maybe in Spain. “Ships of Tarshish” were large ships that sailed the open sea.
The Hebrew words are uncertain. They probably mean moles or shrews.
The Septuagint does not have this verse. The Great Isaiah Scroll does.

verses.text:
Watch! The Lord, Yahweh of Armies,
will remove from Jerusalem and Judah
every prop that holds them up:
the whole stock of bread
and the whole stock of water.{a}

He will remove the hero and the warrior,
the prophet, the judge,
the fortune reader, and the elder,

the captain of fifty and the respected man,
the adviser, the skilled craftsman,
and the expert in spells.

“I will make boys their rulers,
and childish people will govern them.”{b}

The people will pick on each other,
one man against another, neighbor against neighbor.
Young people will be rude to their elders,
and nobodies will insult the honored.

A man will take hold of his own brother inside the family home and say,
“You have a coat, so you can lead us.
This pile of broken stones will be under your command.”

Right then the brother will cry out,
“I refuse to be a healer!
My house has no bread and no coat.
You will not make me the people’s ruler.”

Their faces speak against them.
They show off their sin like Sodom and never cover it.
It is awful for them.
They are bringing disaster on their own heads.

Tell good people it will go well for them,
because they will enjoy the fruit of what they did.

Kids bully my people,
and women boss them around.
O my people, those who guide you send you the wrong way,
and they erase the road under your feet.{e}

Yahweh takes his place to argue the case.
He stands up to judge the nations.{f}

Yahweh comes to put the elders and leaders of his people on trial.
He says, “You are the ones who ate up the vineyard.
What you took from the poor is in your houses.

How can you crush my people
and rub the faces of poor people in the dirt?”
The Lord, Yahweh of Armies, has spoken.

Yahweh also said:
“The daughters of Zion are stuck up.
They stroll along with chins held high,
rolling their eyes at men,
mincing with tiny steps,
their anklets tinkling.

So the Lord will cover the heads of Zion’s women with sores,
and Yahweh will leave them bald.”{g}

On that day the Lord will strip away their fancy things:
the ankle bells, the headbands, and the moon-shaped necklaces,{h}
the earrings, the bracelets, and the veils,
the headdresses, the ankle chains, the belts, the perfume bottles, and the lucky charms,
the finger rings and the nose rings,
the party dresses, the cloaks, the shawls, and the purses,
the mirrors, the linen clothes, the turbans, and the cloaks.

Perfume will give way to a rotten smell.
A rope will take the place of a belt.
A bald head will replace fancy hair.
A scratchy sackcloth will replace a rich dress.
A scar from a burn will stand where beauty was.{i}

Your men will fall to the sword,
and your warriors will fall in the fight.

Jerusalem’s gates will cry and mourn,
and she will sit on the ground, stripped bare.

notes.text: Hebrew ha’adon, “the Lord” (the master). “Everything they lean on” is two forms of one word in Hebrew, meaning “every kind of support.”
Or “babies” or “cruel rule.” The Hebrew word ta’alulim is uncertain.
Or “to rebel against his glorious presence.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll says the payment “will return to him.”
The Septuagint says “tax collectors strip you, and money lenders rule you.” This may come from reading the Hebrew word for “lenders” instead of “women.”
The Septuagint says “his people.” The Hebrew says “peoples.”
Or “their foreheads.” The Hebrew word is uncertain. The Great Isaiah Scroll mixes up “Lord” and “Yahweh” in verses 17-18.
Many of the items in verses 18-23 are rare words, so the exact meaning is uncertain.
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “instead of beauty, shame.” The Hebrew word ki may mean a slave’s brand, or it may just mean “because.”

verses.text:
Seven women will latch onto a single man when that day arrives.
They will say, “We will pay for our own meals and our own clothing.
We only ask to be known as your wives.
Take our disgrace away.”
Those still left in Zion and those who remain in Jerusalem will be called holy. This means everyone in Jerusalem whose name is written down for life.
The Lord will wash the dirt from the women of Zion. He will scrub the blood stains out of Jerusalem. He will do it with a spirit of judgment and a spirit of fire.{b}
Then Yahweh will place a cloud by day over all of Mount Zion and over those who gather there. At night he will place a glowing blaze of flame. A canopy will cover everything glorious.
It will be a shed that shades people from the daytime heat. It will be a hiding place for shelter from the storm and the downpour.

notes.text: Or “the sprout of Yahweh.” Compare 11:1, Jeremiah 23:5, and Zechariah 3:8. The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “and Judah” after “Israel.”
Or “of destruction.” The Great Isaiah Scroll says “of storm.”

verses.text:
Let me sing for my dear friend
a song about my friend and his vineyard.
My friend owned a vineyard
on a rich, fertile hillside.{a}

He dug up the soil and cleared away the stones.
He planted the best grapevines in it.
He built a watchtower in the middle
and carved out a place to crush grapes.
Then he waited for sweet grapes,
but the vines gave only sour, rotten ones.{b}

“You who live in Jerusalem and you men of Judah,
be the judges between my vineyard and me.

Was there anything left to do for my vineyard
that I skipped?
I expected good grapes.
Why did I get bitter ones?

Now I will tell you
what I will do to my vineyard.
I will pull out its hedge, and animals will graze it.
I will knock down its wall, and feet will trample it.

I will make it a wasteland.
No one will trim it or dig around it.
Weeds and thorns will grow there.
I will even order the clouds
to hold back their rain.”

Yahweh of Armies owns a vineyard, and it is the nation of Israel.
The men of Judah are the plants he enjoyed.
He wanted fair courts and saw spilled blood.
He wanted people to do right and heard people scream.{c}

How horrible for you who buy up one house after another
and one field after another,
until nothing is left for anyone else,
and you live alone in the land.

A ten-acre vineyard will make only about six gallons.
A sowing of six bushels of seed will bring in a half bushel.”{e}

How horrible for you who get up early in the morning
to chase after strong drink,
and stay up late into the night
until wine sets you on fire.

You have harps and lyres, drums and flutes, and wine at your parties.
But you pay no attention to what Yahweh is doing.
You do not see what his hands have made.

So my people will be taken away as prisoners
because they do not know me.
Their leaders will starve,
and their crowds will be dry with thirst.

So the grave{f} opens its throat wide
and stretches its mouth without limit.
Down go Jerusalem’s nobles and its crowds,
its noisy parties and all who cheer in them.

People are bent low, and everyone is brought down.
Proud eyes are lowered.

Yahweh of Armies is lifted up when he judges fairly.
The holy God proves how holy he is by acting rightly.

Then lambs will graze as if in their own field,
and wandering kids will eat in the broken places where the rich lived.{g}

How horrible for you who drag your sin behind you
with ropes of lies,
who pull your guilt along like a cart on thick cords.

You say, “Let him rush!
Let him get his work done now so we can watch.
Let the plan of Israel’s Holy One arrive,
so we can find out what it is!”

How horrible for you who label evil as good
and good as evil,
who swap light for darkness
and darkness for light,
who trade sweet for sour
and sour for sweet.

How horrible for you who think you are wise
and believe you are clever.

How horrible for you heroes at drinking wine,
you champions at mixing strong drink,

who let the guilty go free for a bribe
and take away justice from the innocent.

So as fire eats straw
and dry grass shrivels in flames,
their roots will rot,
and their flowers will blow away like dust.
They threw out the teaching of Yahweh of Armies.
They hated the word of the Holy One of Israel.{h}

This is why Yahweh is burning with anger at his people.
He swung his arm and hit them.
The mountains shook,
and corpses lay like garbage on the roads.
In spite of all this, his anger is not over,
and his arm is still swinging.{i}

He lifts a flag for a nation far away.
He gives a whistle for them at the edge of the earth.
Look how quickly they come, in a rush.

No one is tired, and no one stumbles.
No one naps or dozes.
No belt comes undone,
and no sandal strap snaps.

Their arrows are sharp,
and every bow is strung.
The horses’ hooves are like hard stone,
and the chariot wheels are like a whirlwind.

They roar as a lion roars.
They roar as young lions do.
They snarl as they seize their victim
and drag it away, with no one to save it.

In those days they will snarl at Israel
like the sea crashing.
A person looking over the land will see only dark and distress,
and the light itself will go black behind clouds.

notes.text: Or “the song of my dear friend.” The Hebrew says “on a horn, a son of oil,” which means a rich hillside.
The Hebrew word means “stinking things,” so rotten or worthless grapes.
This is a play on words in Hebrew. “Justice” is mishpat, but he found “killing,” mispach. “Right living” is tsedaqah, but he heard “cries of pain,” tse’aqah.
Hebrew “In my ears, Yahweh of Armies.” The words “swear this” are added. Compare 22:14. The Septuagint says “these things came to the ears of the Lord of Armies.”

Hebrew “ten teams of vineyard will give one bath, and a homer of seed will give an ephah.” A team was the land two oxen could plow in a day. A bath was about 6 gallons (22 liters). A homer was about 6 bushels (220 liters). An ephah was about 3/5 of a bushel (22 liters).
Hebrew Sheol, the place of the dead. The Septuagint says Hades.
Hebrew gerim, “strangers.” Some read gedayim, “young goats.” The Septuagint says “lambs will feed in the empty places of those taken away.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll says “and flaming fire” in place of “dry grass in the flame.”
This line comes back at 9:12, 17, 21 and 10:4.

verses.text: King Uzziah died, and that same year I saw the Lord. He sat on a tall, lofty throne, and the hem of his robe spread out and filled the Temple.{a}
Winged beings called seraphim{b} stood over him. Each had six wings. Two wings hid the face, two hid the feet, and two kept the being in the air.
The doorframes shook from the sound of their voices, and smoke filled the house.
I cried out, “I am doomed!{d} I am a man with dirty lips, and I live among people with dirty lips. Yet I have seen the King, Yahweh of Armies, with my own eyes.”
One seraph flew over to me. He held a red-hot coal that he had lifted from the altar with a pair of tongs.
He pressed it to my lips and said, “See, this touched your mouth. Your wrong is gone, and your sin is cleansed.”
Then I heard the Lord ask, “Who can I send? Who will go for us?” I answered, “I am here. Send me!”

He said, “Go and tell these people:
‘Keep listening, but never understand.
Keep looking, but never see.’

Make these people’s minds thick.
Make their ears slow.
Shut their eyes.
Otherwise their eyes might see,
their ears might hear,
and their minds might understand,
and they might turn around and be healed.”{e}

I asked, “Lord, how long?” He said,
“Until the towns are wrecked and empty,
the houses have no people,
and the fields are a barren waste.

Yahweh will drive everyone far off,
and the country will hold a great many empty places.

Even if one tenth stays,
it will be burned again.
It will be like a great oak or terebinth tree
that is cut down and leaves only a stump.
The stump is the holy seed.”{f}

notes.text: This was about 740 BC. “The Lord” is Hebrew ‘Adonai. The “hem” is the bottom part of his robe. Compare John 12:41.
Seraphim means “burning ones.” They are heavenly beings. The same word is used for snakes in 14:29, 30:6, and Numbers 21:6. “Feet” may be a polite word for the lower body.
The Great Isaiah Scroll has “Holy, holy” twice, not three times. Compare Revelation 4:8.
Or “I am silenced” or “I am ruined.”

Matthew 13:14-15, Mark 4:12, John 12:40, and Acts 28:26-27 quote verses 9-10, mostly from the Septuagint. It says, “For the heart of this people has grown dull.” The Great Isaiah Scroll has small differences in verse 10.
Or “when it is cut down.” The Great Isaiah Scroll has small spelling differences, and the meaning is uncertain. The Septuagint does not have the last line.

verses.text: Ahaz son of Jotham, grandson of Uzziah, was king of Judah. Rezin king of Aram{a} and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, marched up to attack Jerusalem, but they could not capture it.
The royal family of David heard the report: “Aram has joined forces with Ephraim.”{b} The king and his people shook with fear, the way trees in a forest sway in the wind.
Then Yahweh told Isaiah, “Go out with your son Shear-jashub{c} and find Ahaz where the channel from the upper pool ends, beside the road to the Washer’s Field.
Say to him: ‘Be careful, but stay calm. Do not be scared, and do not let your courage drain away over these two smoking stumps of firewood, the fierce rage of Rezin of Aram and the son of Remaliah.
Aram has made an evil plan against you, and Ephraim and Remaliah’s son have joined in. They say,
“Let us go to war against Judah and scare it. Let us break it open for ourselves and put the son of Tabeel{d} on its throne.”’

Aram’s head is Damascus,
and Damascus has Rezin at its head.
Sixty-five years from now
Ephraim will be broken up and stop being a people.{f}

Ephraim’s head is Samaria,
and Samaria has Remaliah’s son at its head.
Unless you hold firmly to your trust,
you will not hold on at all.’”{g}
Yahweh spoke to Ahaz again.
He said, “Ask Yahweh your God to show you a sign. Choose anything, from the lowest depths to the highest heights.”{h}
Ahaz answered, “I will not ask. I will not test Yahweh.”
Isaiah said, “Listen, family of David! You already wear out people. Must you wear out my God too?

So the Lord himself will give you a sign.
A young woman is going to have a baby.
She will bear a son
and call him Immanuel.{i}

He will eat curds and honey
by the time he is old enough to refuse evil and pick good.{j}
Before the boy is old enough to refuse evil and pick good, the land of the two kings who frighten you will be left empty.
Yahweh is about to send you, your people, and your royal family a time of trouble worse than any since Ephraim split off from Judah. He is sending the Assyrian king.{k}
Then, on that day, Yahweh will whistle. Flies from the far-off branches of the Nile in Egypt will answer, and so will bees from Assyria.
They will all arrive and settle in the steep valleys, the cracks in the cliffs, every thorn bush, and every water hole.{l}

When that day comes, the Lord will use a razor he rented from across the River. That razor is the king of Assyria. He will shave your head and the hair on your legs, and he will trim off your beard too.{m}
On that day a man will keep one young cow and two sheep.
There will be so much milk that he will eat curds. Everyone who remains in the land will eat curds and honey.
On that day every spot that had a thousand vines worth about twenty-five pounds of silver{n} will fill up with weeds and thorns.
Hunters with bows and arrows will go in there, because all the land will be thorny.
No one will visit the hills that were once dug with hoes, for fear of the briers and thorns. They will become a place to turn cattle loose and let sheep wander.

notes.text: Ahaz ruled about 735-715 BC. Aram is the land of Syria. Its king Rezin’s name may mean “delight.” Pekah means “he opened (his eyes).” Remaliah may mean “Yahweh has decorated.” This war happened around 734 BC. See 2 Kings 16.
Ephraim means “doubly fruitful.” Here it means the northern kingdom of Israel. “Joined forces” can also be “camped in.” David means “beloved.”
Shear-jashub means “a remnant will return.” See 10:21-22. “Washer’s Field” can also be “Fuller’s Field.” Compare 36:2.
Tabeel means “God is good.” It also sounds like a Hebrew word meaning “good for nothing.” He may have been a man from Aram who wanted the throne.
Hebrew ‘Adonai YHWH.

Damascus was the capital of Aram. Samaria, the capital of the north, fell to Assyria in 722 BC. The sixty-five years may count to the time when foreigners were settled in the land. See 2 Kings 17:24 and Ezra 4:2.
This is a word play. “If you do not stand firm (ta’aminu), you will not be made firm (te’amenu).”
Or “as deep as Sheol,” the place of the dead, if the Hebrew is read differently.

The Hebrew is ha’almah, “the young woman.” It means a girl old enough to marry. It is not the usual word for “virgin” (betulah). On its own the word does not say whether she was a virgin. Immanuel means “God is with us.”
Or “yogurt and honey.” These are foods of a land that has gone back to pasture, as verse 22 shows. “By the time he is old enough” can also be “so that he may know.”
Assyria was the great power of northern Mesopotamia. Its capital was Nineveh.
Or “all the pastures.”
The River is the Euphrates. “Hair on your legs” is Hebrew “hair of the feet,” meaning body hair. Shaving was a sign of shame. See 2 Samuel 10:4.
Hebrew “a thousand of silver,” meaning a thousand shekels. A shekel was about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams), so about 25 pounds (11.5 kilograms) in all.

verses.text: Yahweh told me, “Take a big tablet and write on it in plain letters: ‘For Maher-shalal-hash-baz.’{a}
I will call two trusted men as witnesses: Uriah the priest and Zechariah son of Jeberechiah.”{b}
I slept with my wife, the prophet, and she became pregnant and had a son. Yahweh said to me, “Name him Maher-shalal-hash-baz.{c}
Before the boy learns to say “Daddy” or “Mommy,” Damascus will lose its treasure, and Samaria will lose its loot, to the king of Assyria.”
Yahweh spoke to me again:

So now the Lord is about to send against them
the strong, rushing waters of the River.
This is the king of Assyria with all his glory.
It will rise over every channel
and spill over every bank.

It will pour through Judah, flooding all the way.
It will reach up to the neck.
Its wide wings will cover your whole land,
Immanuel.”{e}

Rage, you nations, and be crushed.
Listen, you from distant lands.
Strap on your weapons, and be crushed.
Strap on your weapons, and be crushed.{f}
Yahweh spoke to me with his hand firmly on me. He warned me not to follow the way these people were going. He said,{h}

“Do not call everything a plot
that these people call a plot.
Do not fear what they fear.
Do not panic.{i}

Yahweh of Armies is the one you should call holy.
He is the one you should fear.
Give your awe to him.

To some he will be a shelter.
To both families of Israel, though,
he will be a rock that people stumble over,
a boulder that makes them fall.
To the people living in Jerusalem
he will be a trap, a snare set on the ground.{j}

Many will trip over him.
They will fall and break.
They will be caught in the net and captured.”

Tie up the message and seal the teaching{k}
among my students.

I will wait for Yahweh,
who now turns his face away from Jacob’s family.
I will put my hope in him.
Look at me and the children Yahweh gave me. We are living signs and warnings in Israel from Yahweh of Armies, who dwells on Mount Zion.{l}
Some will tell you, “Ask the mediums and the fortune-tellers who whisper and mumble.” But should people not ask their own God? Should they ask the dead about the living?{m}
Go back to the teaching and the message! Anyone who does not speak by this word has no light of dawn.{n}
They will wander through the land, beaten down and hungry. When they get hungry, they will lose their tempers. They will curse their king and their God and look up toward the sky.
Then they will look at the ground and see only trouble, darkness, and fearful gloom. They will be driven into the blackest night.{o}

notes.text: The name Maher-shalal-hash-baz means “quick to plunder, fast to take the spoil.” It points to the robbing of Damascus and Samaria in verse 4. Hebrew “with a man’s pen” means in ordinary writing.

Uriah means “Yahweh is my light.” He is the priest in 2 Kings 16:10-16. Zechariah means “Yahweh remembers.” Jeberechiah means “Yahweh blesses.” The Great Isaiah Scroll and the Septuagint read this as a command: “Take witnesses for me.”
The “prophet” here is probably Isaiah’s wife.

Shiloah means “sent.” It was the gentle stream that flowed from the Gihon spring (like Siloam in John 9:7). It stands for the quiet rule of the house of David. The meaning of “delighted with” is uncertain.
Immanuel means “God is with us.” See 7:14.
The Septuagint says “Know this, you nations.” Some read “Join together” instead of “Rage.” The Great Isaiah Scroll does not have the last line.
Hebrew ‘immanu ‘el, “God is with us,” the name in 7:14.
The Great Isaiah Scroll says “he turned me away from walking.”
Or “what they honor.” Compare 1 Peter 3:14-15.
Compare Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:8.
Or “instruction” (Hebrew torah). Here it means Isaiah’s teaching.
Compare Hebrews 2:13.
Hebrew ‘ovot and yidde’onim, people who asked ghosts and the spirits of the dead for answers. See Leviticus 19:31 and 1 Samuel 28.
Or “they will speak by this word, but for them there is no dawn.” The Hebrew is hard to read.
In the Hebrew Bible, the first line of English 9:1 is 8:23.

subheads.19: Darkness for Those Who Ignore God

verses.text: Yet the gloom will end for the land that was in pain. In the past he treated Zebulun’s land and Naphtali’s land with contempt. In the future he will bring honor to the road beside the sea, the area across the Jordan River, and Galilee where the nations live.{a}

The people who were walking in darkness
have seen a bright light.
On those who lived in a land of deep shadow,{b}
a light has dawned.

You made the nation grow
and gave it great joy.
The people are glad before you, as at harvest time,
like people shouting as they share the loot.{c}

You smashed the heavy yoke on their necks,
the bar across their shoulders,
and the stick of the one who drove them,
as you did on the day of Midian.{d}

Every boot that stomped in battle
and every robe soaked in blood
will be thrown into the fire as fuel.

We have a newborn boy, a son who is a gift.
Government rests on his shoulders.
His names will be
Wonderful Adviser, Mighty God,
Father Forever, Prince of Peace.{e}

His rule will grow, and peace will never end.
He will sit on David’s throne and rule David’s kingdom.
He will make it strong and hold it up
with fairness and right living,
from now on and always.
Yahweh of Armies is so passionate that he will make this happen.{f}

The Lord sent a message against Jacob,
and it landed on Israel.{g}

All the people will find out,
Ephraim and the people of Samaria,
who say with pride and a stubborn heart,

“Brick walls came down,
but we will build again with blocks of cut stone.
Fig trees were cut down,
but we will plant cedars where they stood.”{h}

So Yahweh stirs up Rezin’s enemies against him
and urges his foes on.

Aram comes from the east, and the Philistines from the west.
They gobble up Israel with wide-open mouths.
Still, his anger has not cooled,
and his arm is still lifted.{i}

The people did not return to the one who hit them.
They did not look for Yahweh of Armies.

So Yahweh cuts off Israel’s head and tail,
palm branch and reed, all in a single day.

The head is the elder and the man of rank.
The tail is the prophet who teaches lies.

The guides of these people lead them down the wrong road,
and the ones they guide are swallowed up.{j}

So the Lord finds no joy in their young men.
He shows no pity to their orphans and widows.
All of them are godless and do evil,
and every mouth talks nonsense.
Still, his anger has not cooled,
and his arm is still lifted.{k}

Evil burns like a fire.
It eats up briers and thorns
and sets the thick forest on fire.
Smoke rolls up in thick clouds.

Manasseh eats up Ephraim, and Ephraim eats up Manasseh.
Then both of them turn on Judah.
Still, his anger has not cooled,
and his arm is still lifted.{n}

notes.text: In the Hebrew Bible this verse is 8:23, and English 9:2-21 are Hebrew 9:1-20. Zebulun means “honor” or “home.” Naphtali means “my struggle.” Galilee means “circle” or “district.” It was the area in the north where many nations lived.
Or “deep darkness.”
The written Hebrew says “you did not make its joy great.” The way it was read aloud changes “not” to “to it,” as here. The Great Isaiah Scroll has “not.”
Midian means “fight.” It was the day Gideon beat Midian in Judges 7. The Great Isaiah Scroll says “Madim.”
Hebrew pele’ yo’ets, ‘el gibbor, ‘avi’ad, sar shalom. It can also be “a Wonder of a Counselor,” “God the Warrior” (in 10:21 the same words name God), and “Father of all time.”
The first Hebrew word, lemarbeh (“his growth”), is written with a final-form letter in the middle of the word. Readers have long noticed this. The Great Isaiah Scroll writes it in the usual way.
The Septuagint says “The Lord sent death,” reading dever (“plague”) for davar (“word”).
Or “mulberry trees,” a common, cheap wood.
Hebrew “Aram in front and the Philistines behind,” that is, east and west. The Septuagint says “Syria from the east and the Greeks from the west.” Compare 5:25.
Or “confused.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll says “does not spare” in place of “does not delight.”
Or “is shaken” or “is burned up.” The Hebrew word ne’tam is uncertain.
Some read “the flesh of his neighbor.” Manasseh means “he makes forget.” Ephraim means “doubly fruitful.” They were the two big tribes of the northern kingdom.

verses.text:
Shame on those who write crooked laws,
and on the clerks who keep recording harsh orders.

They shove poor people away from the courtroom.
They cheat my afflicted ones out of what is theirs.
They make widows their victims
and loot homes where a father has died.

What will you do when the day of reckoning comes,
when ruin rolls in from far away?
Whom will you run to for help?
Where will you hide your riches?{a}

You will have only two choices: huddle with the captives
or lie among the dead.
Even then, his anger is not spent,
and his arm is still reaching out.{b}

Shame on Assyria! It is the rod I use when I am angry.
The club in its fist is my fury.{c}

I send Assyria against a godless nation.
I give it orders against a people who made me angry.
It is to grab the spoils, snatch the loot,
and stamp them flat like mud on the street.

But Assyria does not see it that way.
That is not what its heart has in mind.
It plans to wipe people out
and to chop down nation after nation.

It says,
“Are my commanders not all kings themselves?

My hand has grabbed kingdoms full of idols,
more carved gods than Jerusalem and Samaria ever had.

I did to Samaria and her statues what I did to the rest.
So why not do the same to Jerusalem and her idols?”

When the Lord has finished everything he plans for Mount Zion and Jerusalem, he will deal with the king of Assyria. He will punish him for the pride in his heart and for the haughty look in his eyes.{e}

The king says,
“I did this by my own strength.
It was my own wisdom, because I am clever.
I moved the borders between nations.
I took their stored-up wealth.
Like a bull, I dragged kings from their thrones.{f}

My hand reached into the wealth of the nations
the way a hand reaches into a bird’s nest.
I picked up the whole earth
like someone gathering eggs that were left behind.
Not one wing flapped.
Not one beak opened. Not one chirp was heard.”

Does an ax brag to the person who swings it?
Does a saw boast over the one who works it back and forth?
That would be like a stick lifting the arm that holds it,
or a club picking up a person, as though it were not just wood!{g}

So the Lord, Yahweh of Armies,
will make Assyria’s strong soldiers waste away with disease.
Underneath his splendor a fire will start,
burning like a blaze.{h}

Israel’s Light will become a fire,
and its Holy One will become a flame.
Within one day it will burn up
Assyria’s thorns and weeds.

Only a few trees will be left in his forest,
so few that a child could count them.
When that day comes, those left in Israel, the survivors of Jacob’s family, will quit leaning on the one who struck them. They will lean in truth on Yahweh, the Holy One of Israel.

A few will return, a few of Jacob’s people,
and they will come back to the Mighty God.{j}

Israel, though your people are as countless as sea sand,
just a few of them will return.
A sentence of destruction has been passed,
and it overflows with justice.{k}

The Lord, Yahweh of Armies, will carry out the wreckage he has set,
and it will reach across the entire land.{l}
So says the Lord, Yahweh of Armies: “My people who dwell in Zion, Assyria’s king is nothing to dread. He may hit you with a stick and swing a club at you, as Egypt once did.{m}
In just a little while my fury will be over, and my anger will turn to wiping him out.
Yahweh of Armies will whip him, the way he struck Midian at Oreb’s rock. He will lift his staff over the sea, as he did in Egypt.{n}
On that day Assyria’s load will slide off your shoulder, and his yoke will come off your neck. The yoke will snap because you are well fed.”{o}

They have crossed the pass and said,
“Geba will be our camp tonight.”
Ramah trembles.
Gibeah, Saul’s town, runs away.{q}

Madmenah is running.
The people of Gebim are looking for a place to hide.{s}

Look! The Lord, Yahweh of Armies,
chops off branches with terrible force.
Tall trees are cut down,
and the lofty are laid low.

He will hack through the thick woods with an iron blade,
and Lebanon will fall before the Mighty One.{u}

notes.text: Hebrew “your glory.”
Or “Without me they will huddle.” The Hebrew is uncertain. See 5:25.
Or “Oh, Assyria.” The Assyrian king is the tool of God’s judgment in verses 5-19.
Calno (Calneh), Carchemish (on the Euphrates River), Hamath, and Arpad were cities in Syria and northern Mesopotamia that Assyria took between about 740 and 717 BC.
The Lord here is ‘Adonai.
Or “like a mighty man.” “Wealth” can also be “stores.” The Great Isaiah Scroll does not have this word.
Or “as if a stick could wave the one who lifts it.”
Hebrew ha’adon, “the Lord.”
Or “as when a flag-bearer faints.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
Hebrew she’ar yashuv, which is also the name of Isaiah’s son (7:3). Hebrew ‘el gibbor, as in 9:6.
Romans 9:27-28 quotes verses 22-23 from the Septuagint (“a few of them will be saved”).
Or “in the middle of the whole earth.”
Egypt is Hebrew Mitsrayim, where Israel first lived as slaves.
Oreb means “raven.” He was the Midianite prince killed at the rock named for him (Judges 7:25).
Hebrew “from before oil” or “from before fatness.” It may mean the ox grew too fat for its yoke. Many change the text to “he has gone up from Samaria.” The way the verses divide is uncertain.
Verses 28-32 follow an army marching toward Jerusalem from the north. Aiath is probably Ai, meaning “ruin.” Migron may mean “cliff.” Michmash means “hidden place.”
Geba and Gibeah both mean “hill.” Ramah means “height.” Saul means “asked for,” the first king of Israel.
Gallim means “heaps.” Laishah means “lion.” Anathoth was Jeremiah’s town of priests. The Hebrew word ‘aniyyah means “poor.”
Madmenah means “dung heap.” Gebim means “cisterns” or “trenches.”
Nob was a town of priests (1 Samuel 21-22), within sight of Jerusalem. The Great Isaiah Scroll does not have the word “house” before “daughter of Zion.”
Or “to a majestic one” (‘addir). Lebanon stands for the Assyrian army, since the picture of a forest goes on.

verses.text:
A shoot will come up out of Jesse’s cut-off trunk.
A new branch from his roots will bear fruit.{a}

Yahweh’s Spirit will rest on him.
The Spirit gives wisdom and understanding,
good plans and power,
knowledge, and a deep respect for Yahweh.{b}

Respect for Yahweh will be his joy.
He will not judge by how things look to his eyes,
and he will not decide by what reaches his ears.

He will give the poor a fair trial.
He will make honest decisions for the gentle people of the land.
His spoken order will strike the earth like a rod,
and a breath from his lips will put the wicked to death.{c}

Right living will be the belt around his waist,
and truth will be the band around his hips.

Wolves will be guests of lambs.
Leopards will curl up beside young goats.
Calves, lion cubs, and fattened animals will be together,
and a small child will guide them.{d}

Cows will graze beside bears,
and their babies will sleep next to each other.
Lions will munch hay like oxen.

A baby will play at the hole of a cobra.
A toddler will put a hand into a nest of vipers.

Nobody will hurt or ruin anything
on all of my holy mountain.
The earth will overflow with knowing Yahweh,
as the ocean overflows with water.
In that coming day, Jesse’s root will be a signal flag for the peoples. Nations will seek him out, and his home of rest will be full of glory.{e}

In that coming day the Lord will stretch out his hand once more to reclaim the survivors of his people. They are scattered in Assyria, Egypt, Pathros, Cush, Elam, Shinar, Hamath, and the seacoast lands.{f}

He will raise a signal flag to the nations.
He will gather up the exiles of Israel
and collect the scattered ones of Judah
from the earth’s four corners.

Envy between Ephraim and Judah will disappear,
and those who attack Judah will be cut off.
Ephraim will no longer resent Judah,
and Judah will no longer bother Ephraim.

They will swoop down on the Philistine hillsides in the west.
Side by side they will plunder the desert tribes to the east.
Edom and Moab will fall under their power,
and the Ammonites will take orders from them.{g}

Yahweh will dry up the tongue of the Red Sea.
He will swing his hand over the River with a scorching wind
and break it into seven small streams,
so people can cross in sandals.{h}

A road will lead out of Assyria
for the rest of his people who are left,
just as there was a road for Israel
when they came out of Egypt.

notes.text: Jesse was David’s father (1 Samuel 16). His name may mean “Yahweh exists” or “gift.” “Branch” is Hebrew netser. Compare Matthew 2:23. The Septuagint says “a rod will come up, and a flower will grow from his root.”
The Septuagint adds “godliness” after “knowing” and puts “fear of God” in verse 3. This gives the seven gifts of the Spirit in later Christian teaching.
The Great Isaiah Scroll says “and with the breath of his lips the wicked will be killed.” Compare 2 Thessalonians 2:8.
The Great Isaiah Scroll and the Septuagint say “will graze” in place of “fattened animals.” Compare 65:25.
Romans 15:12 quotes this from the Septuagint: “the one who rises to rule the nations; the nations will hope in him.”
Pathros is southern Egypt. Cush is the Nile land south of Egypt (Nubia). Elam is in southwest Iran. Shinar is Babylonia. Hamath is in Syria. The Lord here is ‘Adonai.
Edom means “red.” It lay south and east of the Dead Sea. Moab lay east of the Dead Sea. Ammon lay east of the Jordan River, around modern Amman.
Hebrew “put under the ban” (or “dry up”). The River is the Euphrates. The word for “scorching” is uncertain. “Red Sea” is Hebrew “the sea of Egypt.”

verses.text:
Then you will say,
“Thank you, Yahweh!
You were angry at me,
yet your anger turned away,
and you gave me comfort.{a}

Look, God is my rescue.
I will have faith and not tremble.
Yah, Yahweh, is my strength and my song,
and he has become my rescue.”{b}

You will happily pull up water
from the wells of salvation.

Then you will say,
“Give thanks to Yahweh and call on his name!
Tell all the nations about his deeds.
Remind them that his name is lifted high.

Make music for Yahweh, because he has done magnificent things.
Let the whole earth know this.{c}

Shout and sing, people of Zion,
because the Holy One of Israel is great, and he is among you.”{d}

notes.text: In verse 1 “you” is singular. In verse 4 it is plural. The Great Isaiah Scroll says “and turned away.”
Yah is a short form of the name Yahweh. Compare Exodus 15:2 and Psalm 118:14. The Great Isaiah Scroll says “God, God is my salvation.”
This follows the way the Hebrew is read aloud. The written form uses a different form of the same verb. The Great Isaiah Scroll does not have the words “let the whole earth know this.”
Or “you who live in Zion,” in a feminine form that stands for the city’s people.

verses.text: Here is a message about Babylon.{a} Isaiah son of Amoz saw it in a vision.

Lift a banner on a bald hill.
Shout to the soldiers.
Wave them forward to enter the gates of the great.

Listen! A sound rumbles on the mountains,
like the noise of a vast crowd!
Listen to the uproar of kingdoms,
nations massing together!
Yahweh of Armies is reviewing
his troops for war.

They arrive from a faraway country,
from the farthest edge of the sky.
Yahweh and his weapons of rage come
to ruin the whole land.{c}

Cry out in grief, because Yahweh’s day is close!
It arrives like ruin sent from Shaddai.{d}

Every hand will hang limp,
and every heart will turn to water.

They will be frightened.
Cramps and pain will grab them.
They will twist like a woman giving birth.
They will stare at one another in shock,
with faces red as flames.

Look, the day of Yahweh is coming.
It is a harsh day of rage and burning anger.
It will make the land a wasteland
and wipe the sinners out of it.

The stars of the sky and their groups, like Orion,
will refuse to shine.
The rising sun will be black,
and the moon will give off no glow.{e}

I will punish the world for its evil
and the wicked for their sins.
I will stop the boasting of the proud
and bring down the pride of cruel people.

I will make human beings harder to find than pure gold,
rarer than the gold of Ophir.{f}

So I will shake the heavens,
and the earth will rattle loose from its place,
on the day that Yahweh of Armies pours out his fury,
on the day his anger blazes.

Like a gazelle chased by hunters,
like sheep that no shepherd collects,
each person will turn back to his own people,
and each will run to his own country.

Anyone caught will be stabbed,
and anyone captured will die by the sword.

Their arrows will cut down the young men.
Mercy for babies? They have none.
Pity for children? Not a drop.

Babylon is the finest of kingdoms,
the beauty and pride of the Chaldeans.
It will become like Sodom and Gomorrah,
which God turned upside down.{i}

No one will ever live there again,
not through all the ages to come.
No nomad will set up a tent there.
No shepherd will let sheep rest there.

Desert animals will rest there instead.
Howling creatures will fill its houses.
Ostriches will live there,
and wild goats will leap around.{j}

Hyenas will cry out in its towers,
and jackals will call in its fancy palaces.
Its time is almost here,
and its days will not be stretched out.{k}

notes.text: Hebrew massa’, “burden” or “message.” It is the heading for the messages against the nations in chapters 13-23. Babylon (Hebrew Bavel) was the great city on the Euphrates River. Genesis 11:9 connects the name with balal, “to mix up.”
Or “those who are proud of my greatness.”
Or “the whole earth.”
Shaddai is an old name for God, often translated “Almighty.” There is a word play in Hebrew between “ruin” (shod) and Shaddai.
The Great Isaiah Scroll uses a different verb, “will not shine.” Compare Matthew 24:29 and Mark 13:24-25. The Hebrew word for “groups” is kesil, which names the star group Orion.
Ophir was a far-off land known for gold (1 Kings 9:28). It may have been in southern Arabia or East Africa.
The Great Isaiah Scroll does not have the last line.
The Medes lived in northwest Iran. They joined the Persians to take Babylon in 539 BC.
The Chaldeans were the people of southern Babylonia. Their kings ruled Babylon in the 600s and 500s BC. For Sodom and Gomorrah, see 1:9.
Several of the animals in verses 21-22 are uncertain. The word for “wild goats” is Hebrew se’irim. It can also mean “goat spirits.” Compare Leviticus 17:7.
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “again” (“will not be stretched out again”).

verses.text: Yahweh will take pity on Jacob’s people. He will choose Israel again and settle them in their own land. Foreigners who live among them{a} will join them and stay close to Jacob’s family.

Nations will lead Israel’s people back to their own place. Then Israel will own those nations as servants, men and women, in Yahweh’s land. They will take captive the ones who held them captive and rule over those who forced them to work.{b}
Yahweh will give you rest from your pain, your trouble, and the cruel slave labor you were forced to do.

Yahweh has snapped the stick of the wicked,
the royal rod of the rulers.

It hit nations in a rage,
blow after blow without a pause.
It ruled nations in anger
and chased them with no one to stop it.

At last the whole world is quiet and at peace,
and people break out in song.

Even the cypress trees are glad at your fall,
and so are the cedars of Lebanon.
They say, ‘Since you went down,
no woodcutter has come to chop us.’

Down below, the place of the dead{d} stirs itself to meet you when you arrive.
It wakes up the ghosts of those who led the earth.
It lifts every king of the nations
right off his throne.

They will all speak up
and say to you,
‘You’ve turned as weak as we are!
You’ve ended up just like us!’

Your pride was thrown down to the grave,
along with the sound of your harps.
Maggots are the mattress under you,
and worms are your blanket.

You fell out of the sky,
bright star, son of the dawn!
You were chopped down to the ground,
you who once knocked nations flat!{e}

You told yourself,
‘I will climb up to heaven.
I will set my throne
above the stars of God.
I will sit on the mountain where the gods meet,
far away in the north.{f}

I will rise over the clouds.
I will make myself equal to the Most High.’{g}

But you were dragged down to the grave,
to the very bottom of the pit.

Those who see you will stare.
They will think about you and ask,
‘Is this the man who shook the earth
and made kingdoms tremble,

who turned the world into a desert,
who tore down its cities,
and who never let his prisoners go home?’

All the other kings of the nations
lie in honor,
every one in his own tomb.

But you were tossed out of your grave
like a worthless branch.
Corpses killed by the sword cover you,
those who sink to the stones of the pit.
You are like a dead body that has been stomped on.{h}

You will not join them in a grave,
because you wrecked your land
and killed your own people.
The family line of evildoers
will never be named again.

Make ready a killing place for his sons
because of their fathers’ guilt.
They must never rise up to take the earth
or cover the world with cities.”{i}
“I will rise up against them,” says Yahweh of Armies. “I will wipe out Babylon’s name and its survivors, its children and grandchildren,” says Yahweh.{j}
“I will turn it into a place for porcupines and a swamp. I will sweep it clean with a broom that destroys,” says Yahweh of Armies.{k}

Yahweh of Armies has made a promise:
“Just as I planned it,
it will happen.
Just as I decided it,
it will stand.

I will crush Assyria in my own land.
I will stomp on him on my mountains.
His yoke will slide off my people,
and his load will come off their shoulders.”{l}

This is the plan for the whole earth,
and this is the hand reaching over all nations.

If Yahweh of Armies has made a plan,
who can cancel it?
If his hand is reaching out,
who can push it back?
The following message arrived the year King Ahaz died:{m}

Philistines, don’t celebrate
just because the stick that struck you has snapped.
From a snake’s roots a viper will come,
and its young will be a flying, fiery serpent.{n}

The poor will graze on the best food,
and the needy will lie down in safety.
But I will kill your roots with hunger,
and your survivors will be slaughtered.{o}

Wail, gate! Scream, city!
Panic, all you Philistines!
A cloud of smoke is coming from the north,
and not one soldier is straggling behind.{p}

What answer will be given to the messengers of that nation?
“Yahweh built Zion,
and the poor among his people will find shelter in her.”

notes.text: Or “the stranger,” meaning a foreigner living among Israel.
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “many” (“many peoples”) and says “to their land and to their place.”
Hebrew madhebah, a word that is not found anywhere else (old translations say “golden city”). The Great Isaiah Scroll has marhebah, “bullying” or “attack.” Many readers choose this reading.
Hebrew Sheol. The ghosts are Hebrew repha’im, the dead. “Led the earth” is Hebrew “the he-goats of the earth,” meaning leaders.

Hebrew helel ben shahar, “shining one, son of dawn.” It is probably the morning star (the planet Venus). Here it mocks the king of Babylon with a picture from old stories in which a bright god tried to climb to heaven.
Hebrew Tsaphon, “the north.” It was also the name of a mountain (Mount Zaphon in Syria) that Canaanites thought was the home of the gods. Or “the mountain of meeting.”
Hebrew ‘Elyon, “the Most High.”
Or “like a rejected shoot.” Some read “like a hated stillborn baby.”
Or “with ruins.”
Hebrew “name and survivor, child (nin) and grandchild (neked).”
Or “the owl” or “the bittern.” The animal is uncertain.
For Assyria see 10:5-19 and 37:36-38.
Ahaz died about 715 BC (some date it 727). Hebrew massa’ means “message.” See 13:1.
Philistia was the land of the Philistines. Compare 2:6. Hebrew saraph me’opheph, “a flying seraph,” maybe a winged snake. Compare 6:2, 30:6, and Numbers 21:6.
The Great Isaiah Scroll says “and I will kill your survivors.” Some read “the firstborn of the poor will feed in my pastures.”
Or “no one is alone at his post.” The Hebrew is uncertain.

verses.text:
This is a message about Moab.
In one night Ar in Moab was wrecked,
and Moab is finished.
In one night Kir in Moab was wrecked,
and Moab is finished.{a}

The people climb up to the temple. Dibon goes to its hilltop shrines to cry.
Moab wails over Nebo and Medeba.
Heads are shaved smooth,
and beards are cut away.{b}

In the streets they dress in sackcloth.
On the flat roofs and in the squares
everyone howls and goes down in tears.

Heshbon and Elealeh cry out,
and their voices reach all the way to Jahaz.
So the armed men of Moab shout in fear,
and their courage trembles.{c}

My heart cries out for Moab.
Her refugees run as far as Zoar and Eglath-shelishiyah.
They climb the slope of Luhith, weeping.
On the road to Horonaim
they cry out over the ruin.{d}

The waters of Dimon are full of blood,
and I am sending still more to Dimon:
lions for the Moabites who get away
and for the ones left in the land.{h}

notes.text: Moab was the kingdom east of the Dead Sea. Genesis 19:37 connects the name with “from father.” Ar and Kir were important cities of Moab. Kir means “wall” or “city.” “Finished” can also be “silenced.”
Or “to Bayith” (which means “the house”). Dibon, Nebo, and Medeba were towns in Moab. Nebo was also a mountain and the name of a god. Shaving the head and beard were signs of mourning.
Heshbon, Elealeh, and Jahaz were towns in northern Moab. The Septuagint says “the waist of Moab cries out.”
Zoar means “small” and was at the south end of the Dead Sea (Genesis 19:22). Eglath-shelishiyah may mean “the third Eglath.” Luhith and Horonaim (“two caves”) also appear on the Moabite Stone.
Nimrim means “leopards,” a stream in southern Moab.
Or “the Brook of Poplars” (or “of the Arabah”). It was probably the Zered, Moab’s southern border.
Eglaim means “two pools.” Beer-elim means “well of the mighty ones” or “well of the oaks.”
Dimon is probably a play on “Dibon” (verse 2) and dam, “blood.” The Great Isaiah Scroll says “Dibon,” as in the Latin Vulgate.

verses.text:
Like birds flapping about,
like a nest that was knocked apart,
so are the women of Moab
at the crossings of the Arnon River.{b}

“Make a plan! Give a ruling!
Make your shade like night
right in the middle of the day.
Hide those who were thrown out.
Do not give away the one who is running.

Let my homeless people stay with you.
Moab, be a shelter for them
from the one who destroys.”
When the bully is gone,
the wrecking has stopped,
and the one who tramples is wiped from the land,{c}

a throne will be set up on faithful love.{d}
Someone will sit on it in truth,
in the tent of David.
He will judge fairly, look for justice,
and be quick to do right.

We have heard how proud Moab is,
very proud indeed.
We have heard about his arrogance, his pride, and his rage,
and about his empty, false bragging.{e}

So let Moab cry for Moab.
Let everyone wail.
You will groan over the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth,
left completely broken.{f}

The fields of Heshbon are drying up,
and so is the grape vine of Sibmah.
Foreign rulers broke down its best branches.
They once reached Jazer
and spread out to the desert.
Its shoots stretched out
and crossed the sea.{g}

So I weep with the tears of Jazer
over the vine of Sibmah.
I soak you with my tears,
Heshbon and Elealeh,
because a war cry has fallen
on your summer fruit and your harvest.{h}

Happiness and joy have been swept out of the orchards.
No one sings or shouts in the vineyards.
No one stomps out wine at the press.
I have silenced the happy shouts.

So my insides moan like a harp for Moab,
and my heart moans for Kir-heres.{i}
Moab will show up at the shrine on the hill and wear himself out. He will go to his holy place to pray, but it will do him no good.
That is the message Yahweh gave about Moab some time ago.

But now Yahweh says, “In exactly three years, the way a hired worker counts them,{j} Moab’s glory will be treated with scorn along with all its great crowds. The few who survive will be tiny and weak.”

notes.text: Sela means “rock.” It was a mountain fortress in Edom (perhaps near later Petra), where Moab’s refugees had run. The Hebrew of this verse is hard. Moab seems to be urged to send gifts to Jerusalem, as Moab once did to David’s family.
The Arnon was the great canyon in the middle of Moab that flows into the Dead Sea.
The Hebrew word for “bully” is hammets and is uncertain. It may mean “robber.”
Hebrew hesed, “faithful love,” God’s loyal kindness to his agreement. David means “beloved.”
Compare Jeremiah 48:29-30.
Or “the foundations” (perhaps “men”; compare Jeremiah 48:31). Kir-hareseth means “city of broken pottery.” It was Moab’s chief city (2 Kings 3:25), probably modern Kerak. See Kir-heres in verse 11.

Sibmah and Jazer were towns in northern Moab known for their grapes. The Great Isaiah Scroll skips from “Foreign rulers” in verse 8 to “the vine of Sibmah” in verse 9, probably because a copyist’s eye jumped.
Hebrew heydad is the shout of people stomping grapes. Here it is the war cry of the enemy. Compare Jeremiah 48:33.
Hebrew “my bowels,” which stood for the feelings. Kir-heres may mean “city of the sun,” or it may be another form of Kir-hareseth (verse 7).
That is, counting the years exactly, as a hired worker counts his time.

verses.text:
Ephraim will lose its forts,
and Damascus will lose its kingdom.
What is left of Aram will end up
like the glory of the Israelites.
This is what Yahweh of Armies says.{c}

On that day
Jacob’s glory will shrink,
and his fat body will get thin.

It will be like a harvester who gathers standing grain
and cuts off the heads of wheat with his arm.
It will be like a person who picks up stray heads of grain
in the Valley of Rephaim.{d}

A few pickings will stay behind,
the way olives stay when a tree is shaken.
Maybe two or three olives
on the topmost branch,
or perhaps four or five
on a fruit tree’s limbs.
So says Yahweh, Israel’s God.

On that day people will look up to their Maker.
Their eyes will turn to Israel’s Holy One.

They will not look to the altars,
the things their own hands made.
They will not pay attention to what their fingers shaped,
the Asherah poles or the incense stands.{e}

On that day their strong cities will be like
the places abandoned in the forests and on the hilltops.
Those were abandoned when the Israelites came,
and the land became a wasteland.{f}

You forgot the God who saves you.
You did not remember the Rock who protects you.
So you plant lovely gardens
and set out cuttings from a foreign god.{g}

On the day you plant them, you make them grow.
By morning you make your seeds flower.
But the harvest runs away
on a day of sickness and pain that cannot be cured.

Listen! Many peoples roar.
They roar like the roaring seas.
Listen to the thunder of nations.
It booms like the crash of mighty waters.

Nations roar like the roar of rushing water,
but he scolds them, and they run far away.
They are blown like straw on the hills,
like a tumbleweed in a storm wind.

In the evening, look: terror!
Before morning they are gone.
This is the share of those who rob us,
the fate of those who loot us.

notes.text: Damascus was the capital of Aram (Syria). Assyria took it in 732 BC.
Aroer may mean “juniper.” Here it may be towns east of the Jordan. The Septuagint says “abandoned forever.”
Ephraim was the northern kingdom, which joined with Damascus (7:1-9).
The Valley of Rephaim lay southwest of Jerusalem. It was a rich valley for grain.
Asherah poles were wooden pillars or trees linked to the goddess Asherah.
The Septuagint says “the Amorites and the Hivites,” instead of “the forests and hilltops.” Many follow this: “like the empty cities of the Hivites and Amorites.”
Or “plants of Naaman” (“pleasant one”). This may be a title of the god Adonis, whose gardens were forced to bloom quickly. “A foreign god” can also be “a stranger.”

verses.text:
Hear this, land of buzzing wings,
far away beyond the rivers of Cush!{a}

You send envoys over the water
in boats of woven papyrus.
Hurry, fast messengers,
to a nation of tall people with smooth skin,
a people dreaded everywhere,
a powerful nation that tramples others,
with a country cut up by rivers.{b}

Everyone in the world,
all who live on the earth:
when a flag goes up on the hills, watch it.
When a trumpet sounds, listen.

Yahweh told me this:
“I will rest and look down from my home,
like heat that shimmers in the sun,
like a mist of dew on a hot harvest day.”{c}

Before harvest time, when the blossoms are over
and the flowers have become ripe grapes,
he will snip off the young shoots with sharp knives
and hack away the wide branches.

All of it will be left for the vultures of the hills
and for the wild animals.
Vultures will spend the summer feeding on it,
and animals will spend the winter feeding on it.

At that time gifts will be brought to Yahweh of Armies
by a people who are tall and polished,
a people feared from their beginnings,
a nation strong, mighty, and overpowering,
whose land the rivers divide.
The gifts will come to Mount Zion, the place named for Yahweh of Armies.{d}

notes.text: Cush was the land south of Egypt along the Nile River (ancient Nubia, modern Sudan). Its kings ruled Egypt from about 715 to 663 BC. “Buzzing wings” may mean insects or boat sails.
Or “tall and bare-skinned,” meaning tall with shiny skin, or shaved. Or “feared far and near.” Hebrew qav-qav means “line-line.” It may mean “mighty” or “measuring.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll does not have “I will rest.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll and the Septuagint say “from a people” and leave out the first “of Armies.”

verses.text:
This is a message about Egypt.{a}
Look, Yahweh rides on a swift cloud
and comes to Egypt.
Egypt’s idols shake in front of him,
and the courage of the Egyptians melts away.

“I will set Egypt against Egypt.
Brother will fight brother,
neighbor will fight neighbor,
city will fight city, and kingdom will fight kingdom.

Egypt’s spirit will drain out of it,
and I will confuse its plans.
They will ask the idols and the spell-casters,
the mediums and the fortune-tellers.{b}

I will give the Egyptians up
to a hard master,
and a fierce king will govern them.”
So says the Lord, Yahweh of Armies.{c}

The water of the river will dry up,
and the Nile will be parched and bare.

Fishermen will mourn.
Everyone who throws a fishing line into the Nile will grieve,
and those who set out nets on the water will lose hope.

Those who work with combed flax will be ashamed,
and so will the weavers of white cloth.{f}

The pillars of the country will be crushed,
and every paid worker will ache inside.{g}

The officials of Zoan are complete fools.
Pharaoh’s wisest advisers give him stupid advice.
How can you tell Pharaoh,
“I am descended from wise men,
from ancient kings”?{h}

So where are your wise men?
Let them tell you now. Let them learn
what Yahweh of Armies has planned against Egypt.

Zoan’s officials have turned into fools.
Memphis’s leaders have been fooled.
The chiefs of her tribes
have pushed Egypt off course.{i}

Yahweh has poured into her
a spirit of confusion.
They make Egypt stagger in everything she does,
like a drunk who slips in his own vomit.
When that day comes, the Egyptians will be as weak as frightened women. They will shiver as Yahweh of Armies waves his hand over them.
Judah will become a horror to Egypt. Whenever someone mentions Judah, the Egyptians will panic, because of what Yahweh of Armies has planned against them.
In that time five Egyptian cities will use the speech of Canaan and swear loyalty to Yahweh of Armies. One of them will be known as the City of the Sun.{k}
In that time Yahweh will have an altar in the heart of Egypt and a stone pillar at its border.{l}
They will stand as a sign and a witness to Yahweh of Armies in Egypt. When the Egyptians call to Yahweh because of their oppressors, he will send them a rescuer, a champion, who will save them.{m}
Yahweh will reveal himself to the Egyptians, and in that time they will know him. They will worship with sacrifices and gifts, and they will make promises to him and carry them out.
Yahweh will hit Egypt hard, and then he will heal it. The Egyptians will return to Yahweh. He will hear their requests and make them well.
In that time a highway will link Egypt and Assyria. Assyrians will go into Egypt, and Egyptians will go into Assyria. Together they will serve Yahweh.{n}
In that time Israel will join Egypt and Assyria as the third, bringing blessing to the middle of the earth.
Yahweh of Armies will bless them and say, “Blessed be Egypt, my people. Blessed be Assyria, whom my hands made. Blessed be Israel, my own possession.”{o}

notes.text: Egypt is Hebrew Mitsrayim.
Hebrew ‘ittim, maybe “ghosts” or “whisperers.” Compare 8:19.
Hebrew ha’adon, “the Lord.” The “cruel master” may be an Assyrian or a Cushite ruler.
Hebrew “the rivers,” meaning the Nile branches and canals in the delta. “Streams of Egypt” is Hebrew ye’ore matsor, a name for Egypt.
Hebrew ye’or, the Nile. Or “the reeds by the Nile.”
Or “will turn pale.” The Great Isaiah Scroll says “and they will be ashamed.”
Or “her weavers.” The Hebrew word for “people who hold up the country” (shatoteyha) is uncertain and may mean “weavers.”
Zoan (Greek Tanis) was a royal city in the northeast delta. Pharaoh is Egyptian for “great house,” the title of Egypt’s king.
Hebrew Noph, which is Memphis, the old capital near modern Cairo.
Hebrew ‘ir haheres, “city of destruction,” which may be a play on words. The Great Isaiah Scroll, some Hebrew copies, and the Latin Vulgate read ‘ir heres, “City of the Sun” (Heliopolis).
A pillar (Hebrew matsevah) was an upright stone that marked a holy place.
The Great Isaiah Scroll says “and he will come down” in place of “and a defender.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll does not have the second “Egypt” (“and Egyptians to Assyria”).
Or “my property.”

verses.text: King Sargon of Assyria sent his army’s top commander to Ashdod, and the commander fought against Ashdod and took it.{a}
Right then Yahweh gave a message through Isaiah son of Amoz. He said, “Go and untie the sackcloth from your waist. Take off your sandals.” Isaiah obeyed and walked around undressed and barefoot.{b}
Then Yahweh said, “My servant Isaiah has walked around undressed and barefoot for three years. It is a sign and a warning about Egypt and Cush.{c}
In the same way the king of Assyria will march off Egypt’s captives and Cush’s exiles, young and old, undressed and barefoot, with their bottoms bare. It will shame Egypt.
The people will be afraid and ashamed because they trusted in Cush and boasted about Egypt.{d}
In that time the people living along this coast will say, ‘See what happened to the nation we trusted! We ran to it for help against the Assyrian king, and now how will we get away?’”{e}

notes.text: The commander is Hebrew tartan, the Assyrian title for the army’s top leader. Ashdod was a Philistine city whose revolt was crushed in 711 BC. Sargon II was king of Assyria from 722 to 705 BC.
“Undressed” may mean wearing only a loincloth, like a prisoner.
For Cush, see 18:1.
Or “the one they hoped in.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll says “in whom we trusted” in place of “we ran to.” “This coast” is probably Philistia and the Mediterranean shore.

verses.text:
A word about the Desert by the Sea.
It sweeps in like storm winds across the Negev,
out of the wilderness,
from a land that spreads terror.{a}

I was shown a grim vision:
the betrayer keeps betraying,
and the plunderer keeps plundering.
Go to war, Elam! Surround her, Media!
I am putting an end to all the sighing she caused.{b}

Because of this my stomach twists in pain.
Pangs grip me,
like the pangs of a woman in labor.
What I hear bends me over.
What I see terrifies me.

The table is laid.
The carpets are rolled out.
People are feasting and drinking.
On your feet, officers!
Grease the shields!{d}

The Lord said to me:
“Go and station a sentry.
He is to tell what he sees.

When he spots riders,
horsemen two by two,
men on donkeys,
men on camels,
he should watch closely,
very closely.”{e}

Look, a chariot is coming with a driver and a pair of horsemen!” Then the man announced,
“Babylon is down! It is down!
The carved gods of the city
lie broken on the ground!”{g}

My people, threshed and crushed on the floor,
I am telling you
what I heard from Yahweh of Armies,
the God of Israel.{h}

A word about Dumah.
A voice calls out to me from Seir:
“Sentry, how late is it in the night?
Sentry, how late is it in the night?”{i}

The sentry replies,
“Morning is coming, and night too.
Ask again if you want to ask.
Then come back.”
The Lord told me, “One year from now, counted as a hired worker counts it, all the glory of Kedar will be gone.{l}
Only a few archers, the warriors of Kedar, will be left.” Yahweh, the God of Israel, has spoken.

notes.text: The “Desert by the Sea” is probably southern Babylonia near the Persian Gulf (the “Sealand”). The Negev is the dry land in the south of Judah.
Elam and Media were peoples of Iran who helped attack Babylon in 539 BC. Compare 13:17.
Or “my mind spins.”
That means to oil the leather shields for battle.
Or “chariots,” as in verse 9. Hebrew rekhev means a team or riders, as well as a chariot.
Hebrew “And he called out, a lion.” The Great Isaiah Scroll says haro’eh, “the watchman,” in place of ‘aryeh, “a lion.”
Compare Revelation 14:8 and 18:2.
This means Israel, beaten like grain on a threshing floor.
Dumah means “silence.” It may be an oasis in northern Arabia (Genesis 25:14). The Septuagint says Idumea (Edom). Seir was the hill country of Edom.
Dedan was a trading people in Arabia (Genesis 10:7 and Ezekiel 27:20).
Tema was an oasis in northwest Arabia (modern Tayma).
Kedar means “dark.” They were northern Arabian nomads (Genesis 25:13). The Great Isaiah Scroll says “three years” (compare 16:14).

verses.text:
you noisy city, packed with uproar,
you town that loves to celebrate?
Those of you who fell did not fall to swords,
and they did not die in a battle.

All your rulers ran away together.
They were captured without a single bow drawn.
Everyone found in you was tied up together,
though they had fled far off.{b}

So I said, “Look away from me.
Let me sob bitterly.
Do not try to console me
about the ruin of my own people.”

This is a day of panic, trampling, and confusion,
sent by the Lord, Yahweh of Armies,
in the Valley of Vision.
Walls are broken down,
and cries for help echo off the mountain.{c}

Your best valleys filled with chariots,
and horsemen lined up at the gate.

You saw how many cracks the walls of David’s city had.
You collected water in the lower pool.

You counted the houses of Jerusalem,
and you tore houses down to strengthen the wall.

You built a tank between the two walls
for water from the old pool.
But you never looked to the one who did this.
You never noticed the one who planned it long ago.{f}

On that day the Lord, Yahweh of Armies,
called for crying and mourning,
for shaved heads and sackcloth.

Instead there was joy and partying.
People killed cattle and slaughtered sheep,
ate meat and drank wine.
They said, “Let’s eat and drink,
for tomorrow we die.”{g}

Yahweh of Armies told me this in secret:
“You will never be forgiven for this sin until you die,”
says the Lord, Yahweh of Armies.
This is what the Lord, Yahweh of Armies, says: “Go to this manager, Shebna, who runs the palace, and tell him:{h}

‘What are you doing here, and who gave you a right to be here,
that you dug a tomb for yourself here,
cutting your grave high on the hill
and carving a resting place in the rock?

Listen, you man. Yahweh is about to throw you far away,
and he will grab you tight.

He will wind you up tightly like a ball
and fling you into a broad country.
You will die there,
and there your showy chariots will sit,
you disgrace to your master’s house.

I will shove you out of your office,
and he will drag you down from your place.’
When that day comes, I will summon my servant Eliakim, Hilkiah’s son.{i}

I will dress him in your robe
and wrap your belt around him.
I will give him your authority.
He will be a father figure for the people of Jerusalem
and for Judah’s household.

I will drive him in like a peg in solid ground,
and he will be a seat of honor for his father’s family.{k}
They will hang all the weight of his father’s family on him: the children and the grandchildren, all the small dishes, from bowls to jars.

When that day comes,” says Yahweh of Armies, “the peg that was driven into solid ground will work loose. It will be chopped off and drop, and everything hanging on it will be wrecked.” Yahweh has said it.

notes.text: The Valley of Vision seems to be Jerusalem itself, perhaps the Hinnom or Kidron valley, where prophets saw visions.
Or “without a bow being drawn.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll differs in the last two lines. It may say “tearing down his holy place on the mountain.”
Elam: see 21:2. Kir was a land whose location is uncertain. Compare 2 Kings 16:9 and Amos 9:7.
The House of the Forest of Lebanon was Solomon’s weapon storehouse (1 Kings 7:2 and 10:17).
Compare 2 Kings 20:20 and 2 Chronicles 32:3-5, 30, about Hezekiah’s water projects. The “old pool” may be the Pool of Siloam.
Paul quotes this in 1 Corinthians 15:32.
Shebna was an official under King Hezekiah and later his secretary (36:3). His name may be short for Shebaniah, “Yahweh has returned” (?). “Manager” is Hebrew soken.
Eliakim means “God raises up.” Hilkiah means “my portion is Yahweh.” Compare 36:3.
Compare Revelation 3:7.
Or “a nail,” a tent peg or wall peg for hanging things.

verses.text:
Here is a word about Tyre.{a}
Cry out, you ships from Tarshish!
Your home port is gone, with no house and no harbor.
The news reached you from the land of Kittim.

Hush, you who live along the coast,
you traders of Sidon,
whose sailors crossed the sea
and made you rich.{b}

Across the deep seas came Shihor’s grain,
the Nile’s harvest.
That was Tyre’s profit,
and she was the nations’ trading post.{c}

Be ashamed, Sidon, for the ocean has spoken,
the sea’s own stronghold says:
“I never went into labor or gave birth.
I never raised sons
or brought up daughters.”

When Egypt hears the news,
they will writhe in pain over Tyre’s fate.

Cross over to Tarshish.
Wail, all you who live on the coast.

Is this the happy city you knew,
whose roots go back to ancient times,
whose own feet carried her to settle in far countries?

Who planned this against Tyre,
the city that handed out crowns,
whose traders were princes,
whose merchants were the great of the earth?

Yahweh of Armies planned it.
He meant to dirty the pride of every splendid thing
and to bring shame on all the honored of the earth.

Yahweh stretched his hand over the sea
and shook its kingdoms.
He gave an order about Canaan
to wreck its fortresses.{e}

He said, “You will never celebrate again,
crushed daughter of Sidon.
Get up and cross over to Kittim.
Even there you will find no rest.”{f}

Look at the land of the Chaldeans!
These were people who were nobody.
Assyria turned it into a home for desert animals.
Assyria built siege towers,
stripped her palaces,
and turned her into rubble.{g}

Cry out, you ships from Tarshish,
for your fortress is wrecked.
On that day Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years, which is the lifetime of one king. After seventy years, Tyre will be like the woman in the song about the prostitute:{h}

“Take up your harp
and stroll through the town,
you forgotten prostitute.
Play it well.
Sing song after song,
so people will remember you.”
When the seventy years end, Yahweh will turn to Tyre. She will go back to earning her pay, selling herself to all the kingdoms of the earth.
But her profits and her pay will be set apart for Yahweh. They will not be saved up or stored. Her earnings will go to those who live in Yahweh’s presence, to buy plenty of food and fine clothes.{i}

notes.text: Tyre was a rich harbor city on the coast of what is now Lebanon. The name means “rock.”
Sidon, “fishing” (?), was the sister port city of Tyre.
Shihor is a name for the Nile, from Egyptian “waters of Horus.”
Tarshish was a far-off port in the west, probably Spain. The Hebrew of this verse is hard to read.
Canaan here means Phoenicia, the coast of Tyre and Sidon.
Kittim means Cyprus. Hebrew calls the city “daughter of Sidon,” and “virgin” is used as a poetic title.
Some ancient copies read a little differently. The Chaldeans were the people of southern Babylonia. The Hebrew is hard to read.
Seventy years may be a round number for the length of time of a king’s rule. The song is not found elsewhere.
Hebrew “holy to Yahweh.” The Hebrew word for “pay” can mean the wages of a prostitute.

verses.text:
It will be the same for everyone:
the priest and the people,
the servant and his master,
the maid and her mistress,
the buyer and the seller,
the lender and the borrower,
the one owed and the one who owes.
